title: Major Arcana vs. Minor Arcana Explained | Spellful
description: Learn the difference between tarot's 22 Major Arcana cards and 56 Minor Arcana cards, including suits and court cards.
h1: Major Arcana vs. Minor Arcana Explained
intro: A standard tarot deck has 78 cards, but not all cards are organized in the same way. The 22 Major Arcana and 56 Minor Arcana provide two complementary layers of symbolism. Learning their structure makes readings easier to follow, even before you memorize individual meanings.

sections.heading: The Major Arcana: broad themes
sections.body: The Major Arcana runs from The Fool, often numbered zero, through The World, usually numbered twenty-one. Cards such as The Magician, The Empress, The Hermit, Death, and The Star are often interpreted as archetypal themes, transitions, or significant lessons. A Major Arcana card does not mean a dramatic event is guaranteed; it may simply suggest that a question feels important or personally meaningful.

sections.heading: The Minor Arcana: everyday situations
sections.body: The Minor Arcana has four suits with 14 cards each: Ace through Ten plus Page, Knight, Queen, and King in many decks. These cards are commonly associated with ordinary experiences, habits, decisions, relationships, and practical concerns. The distinction is not "important" versus "unimportant"; everyday choices can matter deeply.

sections.heading: Four suits and their traditional associations
sections.body: Wands are often linked to initiative, creativity, ambition, and energy. Cups commonly relate to emotion, connection, and imagination. Swords often concern ideas, conflict, decisions, and communication. Pentacles tend to represent resources, work, the body, and material life. Some decks rename the suits, so consult the deck's own guide.

sections.heading: What do the numbers mean?
sections.body: Readers often use numbers as a second layer of symbolism: Aces as beginnings, Twos as choices or balance, Threes as development, and Tens as completion or culmination. These patterns are interpretive shortcuts rather than rigid definitions. The artwork and position in the spread still matter.

sections.heading: Court cards: people or qualities?
sections.body: Pages, Knights, Queens, and Kings can be read as personalities, roles, approaches, or stages of development. A Queen does not have to represent a woman, and a King does not have to represent a man. Consider the card's behavior or quality rather than assigning fixed gender roles or claiming to identify a particular person.

sections.heading: Practice with one of each
sections.body: Draw one Major Arcana card and one Minor Arcana card. Ask how a broad theme and an everyday action might relate. For example, The Star paired with Eight of Pentacles might prompt reflection on hope sustained through steady practice. Write your own interpretation before reading a guidebook.

sections.heading: Remember the limits
sections.body: Tarot meanings differ across historical and contemporary traditions. Use the cards to explore possibilities and values, not to assert certainty about future events or other people's intentions.
